"It is not a 'swine' flu, and people need to stop calling it that ... they're ruining people's lives."

WASECA, Minnesota (CNN) — When people think about protection from the H1N1 flu virus, they may not immediately think of the hog population as the group in need of safeguarding. Yet that is precisely the concern among pork producers and researchers who work with swine.

Professor Samuel Baidoo wears specially issued protective gear as he checks on the hogs at the research facility. And for anyone worried about catching the disease often referred to as “swine flu” from a pig, Baidoo says the greater concern is actually the reverse.

“If we are sick and we come in here, we can easily transfer [diseases], especially flu, to these pigs,” says Baidoo, a University of Minnesota professor and swine nutrition and management expert at one of the school’s swine research facilities.

Baidoo took CNN on a tour of the university’s research facility to demonstrate the precautions in place year-round to ensure that its pig population remains safe. For starters, anyone who wants to visit the facility must shower and put on specially issued overalls and boots—and that rule applies to reporters as well as to the hog farmers themselves.

“They will shower to go and see their own pigs,” Baidoo says.

The university’s swine research barn is typical of most large-scale hog production facilities, Baidoo says, emphasizing that it is so secure that “flies cannot even come in here.”

“Flu can be transferred by flies, by birds. There’s no way a bird can get into this building. So these pigs are very, very safe,” he explains. “We are more a risk to them than they to us.”

So what happens if a pig does contract a disease—specifically H1N1? Baidoo says the first sign that something is wrong is usually a loss of appetite.

“They go off feed, so we know there’s something not right.”

If the illness does turn out to be a flu virus, Baidoo says, the treatment is very similar to what humans receive.

“We put them on medication and within three days it’s over. Just like when we get [the] flu—we go to the doctor and then they prescribe medication and we get well.”

Baidoo points out that because H1N1 is a respiratory illness, the actual carcass of the pig—the pork people eat—remains harmless.

Still, he says he understands the initial, knee-jerk reaction. After all, “swine flu” was the term widely used at first, before health organizations began referring to the illness as H1N1.

“I also see the concern of consumers. When there is this situation everybody tends to connect the two. But there is no connection at all between the flu and pork,” he says. “There’s no fear in eating pork based on the scare of the flu pandemic.”

The disease most people in the United States and around the world have been calling swine flu is actually a combination of human and animal strains. It has not been shown to be transmissible through eating pork.

In a market that is already struggling, the U.S. pork industry says the negative publicity could have been prevented.

“This flu is being called something that it isn’t, and it’s hurting our entire industry,” Dave Warner, communications director for the National Pork Producers Council, said last week. “It is not a ‘swine’ flu, and people need to stop calling it that ... they’re ruining people’s lives.”

“Flu can be transferred by flies, by birds. There’s no way a bird can get into this building. So these pigs are very, very safe,” he explains. “We are more a risk to them than they to us.”

If a pig does become ill, including with H1N1, Baidoo says the first warning sign is often that it stops eating.

“They go off feed, so we know there’s something not right.”

Even so, he says he understands why consumers may have reacted with concern at first. The illness was initially widely labeled “swine flu,” before health agencies began using the name H1N1.

“I also see the concern of consumers. When there is this situation everybody tends to connect the two. But there is no connection at all between the flu and pork,” he says. “There’s no fear in eating pork based on the scare of the flu pandemic.”

The illness that many people in the United States and around the world have referred to as swine flu is actually made up of a mix of human and animal virus strains. There is no evidence that it can be spread by eating pork.

The National Pork Producers Council has also urged producers to maintain strong biosecurity programs and to work with veterinarians and state animal-health officials when illness is suspected. # You Can’t Catch H1N1 from Eating Pork, Experts Emphasize During Hog Barn Tour

Visitors touring a University of Minnesota hog research barn are reminded of a message public health officials and pork producers have repeated since the early days of the H1N1 outbreak: people do not catch H1N1 influenza from eating pork.

The virus that became widely known as “swine flu” spreads from person to person through respiratory droplets, much like seasonal influenza. It is not a foodborne illness. Properly handled and cooked pork remains safe to eat, and health officials have stressed that there is no evidence people can become infected with H1N1 by consuming pork or pork products.

That point was underscored during a tour of a University of Minnesota hog research facility, where visitors got a close look at the measures used to protect both animals and people. Before entering the barn, visitors were required to follow strict biosecurity precautions. These typically include wearing protective coveralls, boots or boot covers, and sometimes masks or gloves. Guests may also be asked to wash hands, avoid contact with pigs before the visit, and stay away from the barn if they have flu-like symptoms.

Such precautions are standard in modern swine facilities and are designed to reduce the risk of carrying disease into or out of the barn. Pigs, like humans, can contract influenza viruses, so preventing the spread of germs is a priority for researchers and producers alike.

The tour also highlighted a major frustration for the pork industry: the name “swine flu.” Industry representatives have argued that the term unfairly links the illness to pigs and pork, even though the 2009 H1N1 virus was spreading primarily among people. They worried the label could mislead consumers into thinking pork was unsafe, hurting farmers, processors, and rural communities dependent on pork production.

Because of those concerns, government agencies and agricultural groups encouraged use of the more accurate term “H1N1 influenza” rather than “swine flu.” The distinction matters, industry officials say, because consumer confidence can be damaged quickly by confusing language.

The key message from public health experts, researchers, and pork producers is straightforward: H1N1 is a respiratory virus, not a pork-related food safety risk. Eating properly cooked pork does not cause H1N1, and standard biosecurity practices in research barns and farms help protect both animals and the public.

**Minnesota hog farms tighten biosecurity amid H1N1 concerns**

**MANKATO, Minnesota (CNN-style report)** — On hog farms across southern Minnesota, the daily routine begins before workers ever enter a barn: a shower, a change of clothes, and a strict reminder that germs can move as easily as people do.

As concerns about H1N1 influenza circulate, pork producers say they are reinforcing biosecurity rules designed to protect both animals and farm employees. Many large operations already use a “shower-in, shower-out” system, requiring workers and visitors to remove street clothes, shower on arrival, and put on farm-only clothing and boots before entering pig barns. When leaving, they shower again and change back into clean clothes.

Inside the barns, workers often wear protective coveralls, gloves, masks or respirators, and dedicated boots. Some farms also limit visitors, disinfect equipment and vehicles, and require downtime for anyone who has recently been around other livestock.

Farm managers say the precautions are not new, but H1N1 has put them under a brighter spotlight.

“If someone is sick, we don’t want them in the barn,” one Minnesota producer said. “The goal is to keep influenza out — whether it’s coming from people or animals.”

Veterinarians say pigs that show signs of flu — such as coughing, fever, loss of appetite, or lethargy — are typically separated from the herd when possible, monitored closely, and given supportive care. That may include making sure they have easy access to water and feed, reducing stress, and treating secondary bacterial infections with veterinary-approved medications when needed. Antiviral drugs used in humans are not routinely used in pigs, and any treatment is overseen by a veterinarian.

Industry representatives are also pushing back on the term “swine flu,” saying it wrongly suggests that pork products or pigs are the primary threat. They note that H1N1 viruses can contain genetic material from human, bird, and swine influenza strains, and that properly handled and cooked pork is not considered a source of infection.

Calling it “swine flu,” they argue, can damage consumer confidence and unfairly harm hog farmers, even when there is no evidence that eating pork spreads the virus.

Public health officials say the key message is prevention: people who are sick should avoid contact with animals, farm workers should follow biosecurity rules, and anyone around livestock should wash hands frequently and use protective gear when appropriate.

For Minnesota’s hog industry — one of the largest in the country — the response is both a health measure and a matter of protecting livelihoods. As one producer put it, “Healthy workers and healthy pigs go together.”

**At Minnesota swine barn, a flu myth meets the facts**

At a University of Minnesota swine research facility, Samuel Baidoo knows that the first sound visitors notice is usually the pigs.

The second thing they notice is the biosecurity.

Before anyone gets close to the animals, there are rules: clean boots, protective clothing, hand-washing, controlled entry. Those precautions are not just to protect people from pigs. They are also to protect pigs from people.

That point is often lost in the public memory of H1N1 influenza, especially after the 2009 pandemic strain was widely labeled “swine flu.” The nickname stuck, and so did a misconception: that ordinary contact with pigs was a major way people became infected.

In reality, public health and veterinary experts have long emphasized that the 2009 H1N1 virus spread primarily from person to person, not from pigs to people. Although influenza viruses can move between species under certain conditions, the main risk during human flu season is often the reverse of what many people assume: humans can carry flu viruses into barns and infect pigs.

For Baidoo, who works closely with swine at the University of Minnesota, that makes prevention a daily responsibility. A cough, fever or “just a cold” in a person can become a herd-health concern if someone enters a facility while ill. Workers and researchers are encouraged to stay away when they have flu-like symptoms, follow strict sanitation practices and limit unnecessary contact.

Pigs can get influenza, and some strains circulate in swine populations. On rare occasions, variant flu viruses associated with pigs have infected people, most often after close exposure at fairs or farms. But those cases are not the same as the widespread human-to-human transmission that drives seasonal flu outbreaks or pandemics.

That distinction matters for farmers, researchers and the public. The term “swine flu” fueled fear of pigs and pork, even though H1N1 is not spread by eating properly handled and cooked pork. It also obscured a more complicated reality: influenza is a shared human-animal health issue, and viruses do not respect the simple labels people give them.

At facilities like the one where Baidoo works, that “One Health” idea is practical, not abstract. Protecting pigs means monitoring people, equipment and movement in and out of barns. Protecting people means tracking flu viruses in animals and responding quickly when unusual strains appear.

The lesson is not that pigs pose no risk. It is that blame is a poor substitute for understanding.

The animals in the Minnesota facility are part of research aimed at improving swine health, food production and disease prevention. But they also serve as a reminder: when it comes to influenza, humans are not just potential victims. We can be carriers, too.

For Baidoo and others who work around pigs every day, the message is simple: good hygiene, vaccination, staying home when sick and strong biosecurity protect both sides of the barn door.
